newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE - Mexican rebels tap dirt-poor region's woes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Mexican rebels tap dirt-poor region's woes.

text.p: The spray paint on the wall in this southwestern Mexican village is fading but the message is clear: "Long Live the EPR."

Government officials say the guerrillas of the EPR, the Popular Revolutionary Army, are a tiny group of extremists with no popular backing. But signs of sympathy for them can be found in places like Atoyac, a town long torn by political strife an hour's drive from the Pacific resort of Acapulco.

"When the EPR first appeared I walked right up to one of them and said 'Good for you,'" said Maximo Gomez, a radical former Catholic priest who witnessed the rebel group's first public appearance at a peasant rally one year ago.

"I know that deep down people here support them. They are afraid to say it openly because they fear repression, but it exists," Gomez, who is widely believed to have close contact with the armed group, told Reuters.

Atoyac, a hot, tropical town, is the gateway to mountains carpeted by dry bush where EPR rebels and army troops recently fought two battles, killing at least nine people. The clashes, the only such skirmishes this year, kindled fears the rebels might disrupt congressional elections on July 6, but the EPR has since said it plans to allow Mexicans to vote peacefully.
The region has long been a breeding ground for rebellion with a mix of wrenching poverty, peasants hit hard by free market reforms and old-style political bosses backed by strong-armed police.

"Of course (the EPR) has support in areas like this, and it is growing," said Carlos Montemayor, a writer and political commentator who wrote a book called "War in Paradise" about a 1970s guerrilla movement in Guerrero. That rebel army was led by schoolteacher Lucio Cabanas, whose Party of the Poor rose up in revolt and roamed the nearby hills before being wiped out by the army.
FEW TOURIST DOLLARS REACH SQUALID VILLAGES

Most Guerrero residents are still as poor now as they were when Cabanas was killed by troops in 1974. Although Acapulco lies nearby, few tourist dollars make their way from the glitzy hotels to the squalor of the nearby villages. Half of Guerrero's residents lack access to clean drinking water and three-fourths make less than $7 per day. Its people are angry.
"Lucio is dead, but his ideals are still alive," Hilda Gomez, an Atoyac schoolteacher who knew Cabanas, said.

Much of the EPR's support comes from militant peasant groups that have multiplied in recent years, demanding paved roads, free fertiliser and farm credits in the face of economic reforms that left farmers with lower prices for corn and the area's commercial staple, dried coconut.
"We are not the (EPR's) comrades in arms but we respect the path they have chosen," Rocio Mesino Mesino, a leader of a radical peasant group known as the OCSS, said. "They are defenders of the poor."

The EPR first appeared at an OCSS rally on June 28, 1996. Wielding AK-47 rifles, the rebels invoked the memory of 17 peasants massacred by police a year earlier and called for a Marxist revolution to topple President Ernesto Zedillo.

Since then, the EPR has established its guerrilla credentials in blood, launching attacks in several states in which at least 32 people were killed and about 50 wounded. But little is known about them. Thought to number several hundred well-armed fighters, the group is seen as little threat to Mexico's army, which built up its forces following the unrelated 1994 Zapatista uprising in southern Mexico.
OFFICIALS INSIST EPR HAS LITTLE POPULAR SUPPORT

U.S. and Mexican officials have assured foreign investors in Mexico that the EPR has little popular support outside remote regions in Guerrero and southern Oaxaca state. "These people want to make us believe that by sending some kids to Mexico City to hand out press releases they are a national organisation," a government source said. "They are not. They are a local problem and we want to treat them that way."

The rebels have not won the hearts of Mexico's middle class in the way the Zapatistas and their charismatic leader Marcos did in their 1994 rebellion in southern Chiapas state. The Zapatistas' sometimes poetic demands for Indian rights and greater democracy found sympathy among many Mexicans, while the EPR's hardline Marxist rhetoric has frightened them.
"I don't think the EPR has had the response from the people that it expected," Javier Galeana Cadena, Atoyac's mayor, told Reuters. "They are too radical, too violent."
But others say the group has won strength by tapping into the discontent found in the Atoyac region's dirt-poor towns and hundreds of similarly wretched villages throughout Mexico.

"The EPR is better equipped militarily and is extended over a much larger area than the Zapatistas," Montemayor said, adding that the group's appearances in at least six states have shown it can move over large areas undetected by the army or police, counting on support from local villages.
Montemayor believes low-level guerrilla warfare is nothing new to Mexico but warns the EPR is easily Mexico's biggest guerrilla threat in modern times.

"They are not a big threat per se to the army or the country's institutions but it is a key social problem in the south of Mexico," he said. "The government has to stop ignoring the problem. To the extent they try to deny it, avoid it, ignore it, the problem will grow."
